Excluded income is not 'omitted gross income' under IRC 6501(e), so the 25%-omission basis does not attach. Reframe the 6-year recommendation as conservative practice for related-party documentation, not as a consequence of the 25%-omission rule.
Update Source #2: relabel IRS Publication 527 from '2024 edition' to the current '2025 edition' (irs.gov/publications/p527).

accuracyConcerns: FLAWED LEGAL RATIONALE for the 6-year retention recommendation (line 96 and The Numbers table, line 168-169). The draft says the 6-year window is the safer standard 'because Augusta Rule rental income does not appear on your personal return at all.' This misapplies IRC 6501(e)(1)(A) / IRS Topic 305. The 6-year assessment window attaches to income OMITTED from gross income exceeding 25% of gross income stated on the return. Income that is properly EXCLUDED by statute (as Augusta Rule income is under 280A(g)) is not an 'omission' and does not trigger 6501(e). Cornell LII 6501(e) text confirms excluded/disclosed amounts are not counted as omissions. A 6-year conservative retention practice is defensible, but the stated reasoning is legally incorrect and should be reframed (e.g., 'conservative practice given related-party scrutiny' rather than tying it to the 25%-omission rule).

STALE CITATION: Source #2 (line 300) labels IRS Publication 527 as the '2024 edition (covering 2025 and 2026 tax years).' The current edition on irs.gov/publications/p527 is the 2025 edition. The substantive rule (rent <15 days: no income reported, no expenses deducted) is unchanged and correct, but the edition label is wrong and should read 2025.

NON-CANONICAL SOURCES used for several claims: Uncle Kam, fraimcpa.com, sambrotman.com, KMK Ventures, TaxPlanIQ, bpa.tax are practitioner blogs, not canonical (IRS/Treasury/statute/state DOR). Replace with the actual canonical sources already used elsewhere on the page: the OBBBA statute (P.L. 119-21) plus the IRS Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC for the $2,000 threshold, and IRC Section 3406 / IRS Publication 505 for the 24% backup withholding rate. Fix the two Numbers-table rows and Sources entry #10.

Correct the Form 1099-NEC deadline for 2026 payments. January 31, 2027 is a Sunday, so the operative furnish/file deadline rolls forward to Monday, February 1, 2027 under the next-business-day rule (IRC 7503). Update the Key Terms entry, Required Documents And Records, Step 8, the Timing And Deadlines table, the Completion Checklist, and Before You Act, or add an explicit note that when January 31 falls on a weekend the deadline is the next business day.

Fix the mislabeled Section 3509 FICA derivations. In Key Terms, '20% of the 1.53% employee share' should read '20% of the 7.65% employee share, i.e. 1.53%.' In the Numbers table, '40% of 3.06% employee share' should read '40% of the 7.65% employee share, i.e. 3.06%.' The employee FICA share is 7.65%, not 1.53%/3.06%.

Strengthen the OBBBA / threshold citation: cite the specific amended Code section (IRC 6041/6041A) and a working canonical URL (Congress.gov H.R.1 text or the IRS news release) rather than the bare 'https://www.congress.gov (H.R. 1, 119th Congress)' placeholder in Sources entry #11.

Optional accuracy polish: the page asserts 'IRS Publication 1099 (2026)' confirms inflation indexing beginning 2027 — re-anchor that statement to the OBBBA statutory text, which is the actual source of the 2027 inflation-adjustment provision.
accuracyConcerns: FABRICATED SOURCE: The page cites 'IRS Publication 1099 (2026)' three times (Numbers table rows for the $2,000 1099-NEC threshold and the 24% backup withholding rate, and Sources entry #10) as the canonical authority. No IRS publication titled 'Publication 1099' exists. Verified: the real authorities are the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) and the IRS Instructions for Forms 1099-MISC and 1099-NEC for the threshold, and IRC Section 3406 / Pub 505 for backup withholding. The underlying facts ARE correct and independently verified, but citing a non-existent publication directly violates the cat-5 gate language ('Sources cited. Nothing fabricated.').

DEADLINE OFF BY THE WEEKEND ROLL-FORWARD: The page states the Form 1099-NEC furnish/file deadline for 2026 payments is 'January 31, 2027' as a hard date in 5+ places (Key Terms, Required Documents, Step 8, Timing table, Completion Checklist, Before You Act). January 31, 2027 is a Sunday; under the IRS next-business-day rule (IRC 7503) the actual deadline rolls to Monday, February 1, 2027. Not catastrophic (the IRS accepts the Monday), but the page presents a date that is technically not the operative deadline, with no mention of the weekend rule.

INTERNALLY-WRONG MATH LABELS IN THE SECTION 3509 DERIVATIONS: Key Terms says '9.18% for FICA (the full 7.65% employer share plus 20% of the 1.53% employee share)' and the Numbers table says '10.71% of wages (7.65% employer share + 40% of 3.06% employee share).' Per IRM 4.23.8 the employee FICA share is 7.65%, NOT 1.53% or 3.06%. The 1.53% and 3.06% figures are the *products* (20% x 7.65% = 1.53%; 40% x 7.65% = 3.06%), not 'the employee share.' The final totals (9.18%, 10.71%, ~10.68%, ~13.71%) are all correct and verified against IRM 4.23.8, but the parenthetical derivations mislabel the inputs and would confuse a reader who checks the arithmetic.

MINOR: 'Public Law 119-21, signed July 4, 2025' — the OBBBA enactment date and P.L. number are consistent with public reporting, but the page should ideally point to the codified statutory section (IRC 6041/6041A as amended) rather than only the slip-law citation for the threshold; the Congress.gov citation in Sources lists only 'https://www.congress.gov (H.R. 1, 119th Congress)' without a specific section/URL, which is weaker than the rubric's 'canonical URLs verified' standard.

results.title: Year-End Strategy Closeout Kit
requiredFixes: Fix the stale Roth IRA phase-out figures at line 185: replace the 2025 ranges ($150,000-$165,000 single / $236,000-$246,000 MFJ) with the verified 2026 ranges ($153,000-$168,000 single / $242,000-$252,000 MFJ), or state them qualitatively. Do not leave prior-year numbers in body copy even with a confirm-with-advisor flag.

Correct the HSA source citation (lines 383 and 560): the 2026 HSA contribution and HDHP limits come from Rev. Proc. 2025-19, not Notice 2026-05. Cite Rev. Proc. 2025-19 for the limits; reserve Notice 2026-05 for the OBBBA HSA-eligibility-expansion point if referenced.

Resolve the internal date inconsistency in the bonus-depreciation explanation: the Key Terms section (line 54) dates the OBBBA signing as 'July 4, 2025' while the QBI term (line 56) and Sources reference the same act. This is correct (OBBBA was signed July 4, 2025) but verify all OBBBA references use a single consistent signing date and public-law cite (P.L. 119-21).

Add an explicit as-of date stamp near the top of 'The Numbers' section. The Before You Act section says figures are 'as of the date this playbook was last updated' but no concrete date is given; a reader cannot tell how current the verification is. State the verification date (e.g., figures verified against IRS sources as of [date]).
accuracyConcerns: STALE FIGURE (line 185): Roth IRA phase-out ranges are printed as the 2025 numbers ('$150,000 to $165,000 (single) or $236,000 to $246,000 (married filing jointly)'). Verified 2026 figures are $153,000-$168,000 (single) and $242,000-$252,000 (MFJ) per IRS IR-2025-111. The draft does append a '[confirm with your advisor]' flag, so it is not asserted as final 2026 fact, but printing the prior-year numbers in body copy is misleading and should be either updated to the 2026 ranges or replaced with a qualitative statement.

CITATION MISMATCH (HSA, lines 383 and 560): The page cites 'IRS Notice 2026-05 (n-26-05.pdf)' as the source for the 2026 HSA contribution limits and HDHP deductible/out-of-pocket figures. Those limits actually originate in Rev. Proc. 2025-19 (issued May 2025). Notice 2026-05 is the OBBBA HSA-eligibility-expansion guidance, not the inflation-adjustment source for the limits. All HSA dollar figures themselves are correct ($4,400 / $8,750 / $1,000 catch-up / $1,700 / $3,400 deductibles / $8,500 / $17,000 OOP); only the source attribution is wrong.

MINOR (line 385, Standard Deduction table source): The standard deduction figures are correct ($16,100 / $32,200 / $24,150) and Rev. Proc. 2025-32 is the right source, but the head-of-household value $24,150 and MFS $16,100 should be double-confirmed against the table; verified correct in this review against the IRS 2026 inflation-adjustment newsroom release.

NOT AN ERROR but worth noting for confidence: the unusual SIMPLE IRA age-50 catch-up split ($4,000 for standard plans vs $3,850 for applicable/enhanced 25-or-fewer-employee plans) was independently verified as a genuine SECURE 2.0 indexing quirk per IRS Notice 2025-67 / IR-2025-111. The SECURE 2.0 mandatory-Roth-catch-up prior-year FICA wage threshold of $150,000 (line 449) was also verified correct for 2026 (IRS raised it from the originally proposed $145,000 in Nov 2025). Both are correct.

results.title: Year-End Strategy Review Checklist
requiredFixes: Tighten the self-employment tax definition in Key Terms: clarify that the 15.3% applies to net earnings from self-employment (92.35% of net SE income), and that the 12.4% Social Security component is what caps at the $184,500 wage base while the 2.9% Medicare component continues with no ceiling (plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200k/$250k).

Add a '[confirm with your advisor]' marker to the ~$505,000 indexed SALT phasedown threshold, since IRS canonical sources confirm the $500,000 (2025) statutory base and the $40,400 (2026) cap but do not publish a $505,000 indexed phasedown figure. Keep the verified numbers ($40,400 cap, $500,000 base, 30% reduction, $10,000 floor, 2030 reversion) as stated.

Define 'modified AGI (MAGI)' in Key Terms (it drives the NIIT, SALT phasedown, IRA phase-outs, and the new tips/overtime phaseouts but is currently only used, not defined), and add brief inline definitions for 'guaranteed payments,' 'MACRS,' and 'apportionment' where they first appear in the Entity/Payroll/State caveats.
accuracyConcerns: SE-tax description is slightly imprecise: the page says SE tax is '15.3% on net self-employment income up to $184,500, then 2.9% above.' The 15.3% rate actually applies to net EARNINGS from self-employment (92.35% of net SE income), and it is the 12.4% Social Security portion that caps at the $184,500 wage base while the 2.9% Medicare portion continues uncapped. The substance (rate, wage base $184,500, deduct half) is correct; only the base on which the rate is applied is glossed. Verified against SSA Contribution and Benefit Base ($184,500 for 2026) and IRS Topic 751.

The SALT cap phasedown threshold is stated two ways that could read as inconsistent: the body and table cite '~$505,000 MAGI (indexed for 2026)' while also noting '$500,000 in 2025.' The canonical IRS OBBBA transcript states the statutory phasedown begins at $500,000 MAGI (2025) and the cap indexes to $40,400 for 2026; IRS has not published a separate indexed $505,000 phasedown figure on a canonical page. The $505,000 is labeled 'approximately/indexed,' so it is flagged rather than asserted, but it is the one number on the page not directly confirmable on a canonical source and should carry a '[confirm with your advisor]' marker. The $40,400 cap, $500,000 base threshold, 30% reduction, $10,000 floor, and 2030 reversion are all verified.

Minor undefined terms in the caveats section that slightly dent full self-containment but are not accuracy errors: 'guaranteed payments,' 'MACRS,' and 'apportionment' are used without inline definition; 'modified AGI (MAGI)' is referenced repeatedly but never formally defined in Key Terms.
